1:
The date sets the first problem, since the fourth year named here is a third year elsewhere, and four reconciliations are offered. Clarke appeals to a co-regency: the conqueror was associated with his father two years before his death, so the Jews reckon from the association and the Chaldeans from the death. Henry works from overlapping regnal years, the one king beginning to reign alone late in his neighbour's third year, while the fourth had opened before the first was complete. Calvin explains the interval by events, since a father's death called the conqueror home to secure his affairs, and only afterwards did he return to subdue Jehoiakim and carry off the first captives and vessels; a reign shared with a father, he adds, is justly dated from where it becomes sole. Ellicott lets both reckonings stand and fills in the setting: Nineveh had fallen and Egypt had been beaten at Carchemish.

Where the chapter stands is a second question. Clarke says flatly that it is out of its place and belongs among the later chapters. Calvin reaches the same point more mildly, concluding that the book is composed of various addresses in which the order of time is not always preserved. Ellicott notes only that the arrangement carries the reader back to a much earlier period. Keil and Delitzsch leave placement alone and set out the structure instead.

Gill and Henry agree that the prophet spoke not through the country but to as many as he found together, probably at a feast, which Henry turns into a rule: what is of universal concern ought to be of universal cognizance. On the twenty-three years Ellicott gives the arithmetic and notes that this same year apparently saw the first collection of the prophet's utterances. Henry draws the account from it, that God reckons how long we have enjoyed the means of grace. Calvin puts it as loss: the time was spent in vain and much labour consumed without fruit, so the charge is not impiety merely but untameable perverseness.

Rising early draws out Henry furthest: what men are intent upon they rise early to prosecute, and the phrase intimates a heart so set on doing good that it broke the prophet's sleep; morning lectures, he adds, have their advantages. Calvin takes the phrase for assiduity and notes the difficulty when it is applied to God, who neither rises nor sleeps. On the other prophets, Gill and Henry name those whose books survive and Henry adds that many more preached sermons never published, while Ellicott finds evidence of helpers whose names have not come down. Calvin makes it an aggravation: prophecy being an invaluable treasure and pledge of favour, to reject them all was a double crime.

What the message contained is summarised alike. Henry gives four heads: they were told their faults, since those who flattered were not of God's sending; idolatry was named; personal reformation was required, the street not being clean unless every man sweeps before his own door; and obedience would have lengthened their tranquillity, since we never receive the evil of punishment but where we provoke by the evil of sin. Calvin presses the mildness of the terms, since God demanded nothing but repentance and attached a promise of free forgiveness, so that men not harder than stones must have been won. On why idolatry is singled out he answers that other sins show contempt less directly, whereas adopting the superstitions of the nations testified that God was theirs no longer; Gill reaches it from the theocracy, under which protection followed worship. Ellicott notes that the works of their hands were their idols. Calvin closes by reading the last clause as mercy: nothing can be subtracted from God's rights, so a reproof showing that their rebellion turns only to their own ruin proves he would not have them perish.
8:
Sentence follows the charge, and Henry states the principle: those who will not regard the judgments of God's mouth may expect to feel the judgments of his hands. He then draws out the reciprocity. God sent his servants the prophets and they were not heeded, so he sends his servant the king, whom they cannot mock or persecute as they did these; the messengers of wrath go to those who would not receive the messengers of mercy. Wesley puts it in an antithesis, that the conqueror shall be God's servant in this work though they would not serve in obeying his commands.

The title is what they find remarkable. Ellicott notes that the word is used of David and of Christ, and finds a parallel where another prophet calls the Persian the shepherd and anointed of the Lord: each ruler of the great empires was working out purposes he knew nothing of. Henry pairs them, the instrument of wrath being as truly God's servant as the instrument of mercy, the man serving God's designs while thinking he served his own. Calvin hears in the summons a royal edict, by which those enlisted assemble, so that the Chaldeans stand under God's power ready at a signal.

Around this they attend to smaller things. Ellicott takes the families of the north for the mingled races under the Chaldean sway. Gill reads the desolation as taking in not the city only but all Judea, uncultivated and without inhabitants. Keil and Delitzsch correct a referent, insisting that this land means Judah and these nations those around it, against a commentator who extended it further. Clarke raises two textual points, that the Hebrew may be rendered a present rather than a future, and that seven manuscripts read and Nebuchadrezzar for and to Nebuchadrezzar, which he calls undoubtedly the true reading. Calvin observes that the word rendered perpetual is elastic, meaning now perpetuity, now the interval until Christ, and here a long while.

The silenced house draws the fullest comment, and two voices reconstruct the domestic day differently. Clarke joins the millstone and the candle because the corn was ground before daybreak by candlelight, and cites a traveller that the mills may be heard everywhere in the morning, each day's grinding being what that day will consume. Ellicott separates them, making the millstone the grinding by women for the midday meal and the candle the lamp lit when the day's work is over, and says no words could paint more terribly the breaking up of family life, not in its festivities only but its daily routine. Calvin cares not for the routine but the degree: in ordinary adversity marriages are still kept and food prepared, and the loss of all of it marks an extremity beyond common chastisement. Henry supplies the reason within the figure: no candle because no work worth candle-light, and no mirth because they have neither cause nor heart for it.

The seventy years divide them again. Clarke counts from the fourth year of the reign, when the invasion began, reaching the Persian king's proclamation exactly. Ellicott reckons from the deportation of the king and his princes to the decree of return, connects the figure with the land enjoying the sabbaths it had been denied, and notes that seventy, seven multiplied by ten, carries completeness. Henry calls the question a great doubt, since some date from that captivity and others from one eight years after, and inclines to the earlier because the nations then began to serve. He adds that a fixed term was of use both to confirm the prophecy, no human sagacity being able to foresee such a number, and to encourage prayer in the captivity. Calvin alone declines to date it, taking the term for a correction that softens what was just called perpetual desolations and shows the punishment temporary.
12:
The turn against Babylon opens a question about the text, and two voices are flatly opposed. Ellicott suspects interpolation. The clause naming the king is absent from the Greek version of this chapter, which differs materially from the Hebrew; and there are internal grounds too, since a later verse veils the same prediction in enigmatic language, and it is not easy to see why one discourse should carry both the veiled and the open form. At the next verse he finds the trace again, the Greek presenting the words detached as a title and following them with the oracles against the nations that the Hebrew places at the end of the book, and calls the phrase about all that is written in this book manifestly a scribe's addition. Keil and Delitzsch report that three critics pronounce these verses spurious and answer that their main argument is a dogmatic prejudice about what the prophet could have foreseen that year.

The arithmetic of the seventy years occupies the tile next, and no two tallies agree. Gill sets out his own, running the Babylonian reigns through the conqueror's two years with his father and forty-three alone, then the short reigns after, to sixty-nine years and two months, adding ten months more to reach the first year of the Persian; two other reckonings, he says, come to much the same. Wesley assigns thirty-six years to the conqueror where Gill assigns forty-five. Keil and Delitzsch date the fall of the city to the allied Medes and Persians, making the interval from the taking of Jerusalem sixty-eight years. Clarke adds a textual preference, that the phrase rendered that nation should rather be his nation, the pronoun standing in the genitive.

Calvin cares not for the tally but for whom the promise was meant. The time was defined so the faithful might know God had not forgotten his covenant; and the words were not addressed indiscriminately to the whole people but meant for the elect, who would have despaired a hundred times without them, a special doctrine given as food for God's children. On the bringing of all God's words upon the land he presses the idiom: to bring a word is to prove its authority by the event, the expression shaped to men who credit nothing God says until convinced by its accomplishment, thinking till then that the air only is beaten.

The last verse turns the sentence on the conquerors. Gill and Clarke identify the many nations and great kings as the Medes and Persians with their allies. Ellicott corrects the English, since to serve themselves of is a seventeenth-century borrowing from the French, now ambiguous, the sense being to make them their servants; and finds in the retribution the poet's thought of a captured Greece taking her conqueror captive. Keil and Delitzsch read the perfect as a prophetic present and gloss the construction as imposing servitude. Calvin works the same verb at length, rejecting the rendering that they employed them as frigid and ambiguous, since friends may be said to employ one another where the work is mutual, and preferring that they forced them into bondage; the tense, he adds, is open, so read as a past it applies to the Babylonians and as a future to those who would subdue them.

Out of that grammar Calvin draws his conclusion. The conqueror was never called God's servant because he had earned anything; God led him unconscious of it. So though the devil and the reprobate execute God's judgments they deserve no praise for their obedience, having no such purpose in view; and the proof is the punishment itself, for had they been without fault, God must have punished them unjustly. Gill puts the same confidence otherwise, that not one word spoken by the Lord can fail, his truth and faithfulness being engaged to accomplish it.
15:
The cup is where the chapter becomes a vision, and Calvin explains the turn as the author's own gloss: the earlier oracle had spoken of all nations abruptly, without saying the prophet was sent as a herald to summon them before God's tribunal. Relating the vision serves three ends, he says: it adds authority, testifies that he brought nothing of his own, and shows him a witness against the nations as well as a teacher in the Church. Wesley says God made him see the appearance of such a cup, Gill that he took it in a visionary way.

Whether anything was physically done with it draws the sharpest agreement in the tile. Keil and Delitzsch report the question raised, whether the prophet travelled to the various kings or handed the cup to ambassadors in the city, and call the question itself the result of an imperfect understanding: he receives not a flagon of wine to pass round as a symbol but a cup filled with the wrath of God; and as wrath is no essence to be drunk by a bodily act, the cup is no material cup and the drinking no outward act. Ellicott calls the same supposition a strange example of the literalism of minds incapable of entering into the poetry of a prophet's work. Clarke reaches the same end shorter, taking the cup for merely symbolical and the taking of it for a public declaration of the tribulation coming.

On the reeling that follows, Gill has the judgments work as strong drink does. Ellicott makes it something history has often witnessed, the panic terror of lesser nations before the march of a great conqueror, as if stricken with drunken madness, their despair and resistance equally infatuated. Calvin has the refusal anticipated and overruled, since willing or unwilling they must drink what God's judgment has measured; and he traces the sword passing from hand to hand, so that with it they contend against each other until it ruins them all. Henry adds that though they will not believe the prophet he must tell them it is the word of the Lord of hosts and that it is vain to struggle against almighty power.

Calvin turns the taking of the cup into a defence of the man who took it: he was constrained to his office, and being bound to the divine call the fault was not his, prophets incurring much ill-will as though the calamities they announced were their doing. Henry states the consequence: if God's judgments begin with backsliding professors, let not the wicked expect to escape.

Why the list begins where it does is explained four ways. Calvin gives two reasons for beginning at Jerusalem, that a father's solicitude is most evident toward his own household, and that those taught his will are the less excusable. Ellicott agrees on the principle, the prophet passing from the house of God to those without, and describes the order as running from south to north. Keil and Delitzsch trace the route from Egypt northwards through the Arabian and Philistine borders, then Edom and Moab and Ammon on one side and the Phoenicians on the other, then the desert tribes to the Euphrates, then Elam and Media, and last the king of Babylon. Gill explains the second place differently, the judgment having fallen on Egypt first in fact. Calvin explains it morally: Egypt was the occasion of ruin to the chosen people, who turned their hopes there rather than to God when they found themselves unequal to Assyria, so the fountain of their destruction is named immediately after themselves. Clarke adds that this Pharaoh was the chief instigator of the league against the Chaldeans. Ellicott finds one more transcriber's trace in the clause as it is this day, absent from the Greek and probably added once the prediction was fulfilled.
20:
The catalogue is mostly identification, and the mingled people begin it in dispute. Gill takes them for a mixed population in or near Egypt; Clarke for strangers settled there. Ellicott is more precise, noting that the word is all but identical with the one used of the mixed multitude that left Egypt and of the alien population of Jerusalem, and identifying these with the Ionian and Carian mercenaries settled at Bubastis by the Pharaoh's father. Uz all agree lies toward Edom, the scene, Ellicott adds, of the great drama of Job.

The Philistine cities raise a question, since one of the famous five is missing and another appears only as a remnant. Ellicott says the missing city had disappeared from the confederacy, possibly by secession, and calls the remnant phrase characteristic of the prophet's time, the other city having fallen after a siege of twenty-nine years. Wesley attributes that destruction to one of two named conquerors. Calvin, without the history, infers it: the place had been taken but not wholly abandoned, its position being too advantageous, and what remained was delivered to the sword. On the three nations that follow, Gill names them implacable enemies, while Calvin notices what their descent implies, that all three were kinsmen of Israel and grouped together on purpose.

The region beyond the sea divides them three ways. Clarke prefers the marginal reading, the kings of the region by the sea side, the Mediterranean being meant and the Phoenicians having many colonies on its coasts. Ellicott keeps the Hebrew singular and renders it a coast-land, wider than our word island, identifying it probably with Cyprus. Calvin would make the number plural, since it is common Hebrew usage to call all countries beyond the sea islands. He also presses the plural kings of the two cities, concluding that men of more than one age are summoned.

Through the eastern names the voices supply genealogies, and Ellicott adds why the traders are here, their caravans carrying the commerce between Tyre and Arabia; he also corrects the phrase about the utmost corners from the margin, making it those whose temple-corners are shorn, pointing to the nomads of Kedar. Calvin declines the exercise with a confession worth recording: these countries are not known in his day, their extent cannot be learned from geographers, and hardly a place had failed to change its name long before heathen writers began their records. On the desert Arabs he says only that they were petty robbers dwelling in tents, which Clarke also supposes.

Of the remoter kingdoms Ellicott observes that one name occurs nowhere else as a country, and connects it tentatively with a son of Abraham by his second wife, as Gill and Wesley do. Elam, Ellicott says, properly means the region whose capital was Susa but was extended by Hebrew writers to all Persia. Calvin makes the point of the sequence rather than the places: the Medes and Elamites were of great repute, and the obscure nation beside them shows that every part of the earth known to the Jews would be visited, so that the whole earth becomes a witness that God sits in heaven as judge.

The last name is the crux. Clarke takes it for an ancient king of Babylon deified after his death, here standing for either the city or its king. Ellicott, calling it from its position the culminating point of the whole prophecy, notes that no place of the name is known and treats it as a cypher veiling the true significance, reporting other senses. Wesley and Gill simply read the king of Babylon, last of all to drink. Calvin attends to the order: the Chaldeans come last because their king was the instrument by whose hand the rest were punished, and the Jews were to bear the yoke patiently rather than hasten after his punishment.
27:
The command to drink is repeated and made coarse, and the coarseness divides two voices. Clarke registers a complaint about the translators rather than the text, asking why a less offensive word of the same signification was not used. Ellicott defends the word precisely because it offends: it is the one most alien to modern feeling and is significant for that reason, implying that the spoilers of Israel should themselves be spoiled and made to disgorge their prey. He reads the image as terror and dismay of a kind that makes joint action impossible and reduces the nations affected to helpless impotence.

Calvin uses the repetition to explain what kind of speech this is. The prophet did not in fact carry the message round to the nations, and the benefit of the predictions belonged only to the Jews; neither the Tyrians nor the Sidonians ever knew that their plundering was God's hand at work, since the prophet was never appointed their teacher, his duty being to warn his own nation. He is introduced as God's herald denouncing ruin on all the nations so that his predictions might carry greater authority with those who did hear them. Gill takes the address at face value, as spoken to the several nations already named, and Ellicott draws the practical consequence for them, that their wise and safe course, like Judah's, was to accept the punishment and submit.

The refusal in the next verse is anticipated and cancelled. Calvin says the prophet introduces them as refusing in order to make the answer more striking, since willing or unwilling they must drink what has been measured out; men are like unruly horses that kick and rage against the rider, and the point is again for God's Church, that none of those threatened could escape. He notices that the two verbs differ, the first an imperative and the second a future, so the second may be rendered ye must drink. Ellicott gives the same construction more briefly as drinking, ye shall drink. Gill fills in what the refusal consists of, not a refusal to lift a cup but a refusal to credit the prophecies, saying that these things shall not be. Keil and Delitzsch set the verses out together and carry the sense forward into the roar from on high that follows.

The reason given is an argument from the less to the greater, and it is the tile's centre. Ellicott recognises the thought as the apostle's, that if judgment begins at the house of God: this being the chastisement of a chosen people, it followed the more strongly that the less favoured, with fewer claims, should not escape. Calvin puts the same reasoning in his own figure. If God does not spare the city in which he chose a temple for himself and appointed his name to be invoked, how shall he spare aliens to whom he never made any promise and whom he regarded as strangers? If the green tree is consumed, how can the dry remain safe? He notes that the apostle argues the same way, first placing judgment at God's house and then showing how dreadful the vengeance awaiting open enemies must be.

Gill and Clarke keep the historical edge. The city called by God's name is Jerusalem, where his name was invoked, and the judgment had not merely been threatened but already begun, since that very year the siege came and captives were carried off; it was to be given up to destruction first. Calvin closes on the last clause with the doctrine he wants drawn from the whole: it lies in God's power to excite wars and to quell them whenever it pleases him, so that the sword, though it is wielded by the hand of man, is not called forth by the will of man but by a hidden power.
30:
The roar from on high gives Ellicott his sharpest complaint against the English. One word does duty for two Hebrew words of very different meaning, which he calls singularly infelicitous: the first is God's own dwelling, from which the thunder of his wrath is heard, the second the pasture of the flock and its shepherds, on whom the storm falls; and the association may turn the roaring, in the prophet's mind, into that of a lion attacking the flock. The shout that follows he takes from an earlier prophet, the cry of men treading the winepress serving as the war-cry of the Lord of hosts. Calvin works the word differently, noting that some render it a mournful singing and that it belongs to the vintage, and preferring a loud noise; on the roaring he asks against whom it is directed and answers, against himself, since though all combined to extinguish God's vengeance he would come forth conqueror.

Calvin repeats that the prophet was never commanded to go among the heathen, and adds the consequence: though he never moved a foot from the city, his prophecy reached every region of the earth. Henry turns the geography into a reproach: the neighbouring nations might have come to the temple for the knowledge of God and their duty and had reason to bless him for their nearness to it, and instead took every opportunity to debauch or disturb the holy city.

The controversy in the next verse is read by Ellicott as a term of law: it denotes a legal process rather than a debate, and is rightly followed by the technical word for pleading, so that God appears as Accuser in a suit where he is also the supreme Judge. Keil and Delitzsch take the noise for the din of war, and note that the wicked are put first for emphasis and resumed in the pronoun. Calvin allows the word to mean either a sound or an assault, then raises the objection he expects: what does it mean that God should suddenly raise a commotion after lying quiet for ages? His answer is that the time of contending is not always, and one who forbears to bring his adversary at once before the judge deals kindly with him meanwhile.

How the evil travels from nation to nation is genuinely disputed. Gill makes it a contagion, catching like a distemper or a fire that consumes one house and then the next, and traces it through the succession of empires to the Romans. Clarke keeps it narrower, one nation after another falling before the Chaldeans. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott see a storm instead, rising on the horizon and spreading over the nations, the word being the generic one for a tempest. Calvin canvasses the reading that the nations destroy one another and grants it may be admitted, then rejects it at the next verse: the prophet speaks not of slaughters inflicted by one people on another but declares that God's wrath would spread like a storm over all lands.

That next verse settles for Calvin who does the killing. The slain are called the Lord's because the prophet fixes attention on God alone, setting before us not the ministers of his vengeance but God acting by himself, who would not be satisfied with three or four nations but shows himself judge of all countries. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch keep the same reach and dwell on the aggravation, the corpses lying from one end of the earth to the other unmourned, ungathered and unburied. Clarke alone shrinks the compass, taking it from one end of the land to the other and making the desolation Palestine's. Henry closes on the pity of it, that the tender share the common calamity and even those who provoked nobody do not escape, setting against it the peaceable habitation above.
34:
The summons to howl is addressed to shepherds, and who they are divides the tile. Clarke and Wesley take them for kings and chiefs, and Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree, Ellicott adding that the principal of the flock are the best and fattest of the rams, standing for the princes and captains, and Keil and Delitzsch that no rank is spared. Calvin dissents bluntly: he does not doubt the prophet turns here especially to his own nation, a thing interpreters have not observed, and for want of observing it have not understood his meaning. On his reading the passage returns from the nations to the Jews, that they might know they looked for impunity in vain and yet flee to mercy.

Ellicott twice objects to what the translators supplied. At the wallowing he says the italicised words were added to conform the passage to an earlier chapter, are not needed, and leave an unauthorised interpretation where the sense is to roll on the ground. At the cry two verses later he says the insertion is a change for the worse, reducing the Hebrew's dramatic vividness to the tamest prose: the prophet speaks as though he heard the cry of the princes and the howling of the captains under them. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point without the complaint, and add that the word about dispersions is obscure, the received pointing differing from many copies.

On the breaking, Clarke and Wesley reach for the same figure, a precious vessel of crystal or agate which a fall shatters beyond mending. When flight is denied them Gill observes that neither dignity nor power nor riches will open a way, and Calvin measures the loss: it is wretched enough when a man can save his life only by exile, where he must be poor and despised, and even that is refused, the idiom being that flight has perished from them.

The peaceable habitations Ellicott would render peaceful pastures. Gill takes them for stately dwellings laid waste, and adds that those who disturbed nobody share their neighbours' fate. Calvin finds the adjective deliberate. The Jews inferred future safety from enemies not having disturbed them before; and while the faithful rightly argue from past kindness that God will be kind still, hypocrites who never repent absurdly conclude that he is bound to them, and go on securely while daily provoking him.

The lion leaving his covert closes the chapter and is read three ways. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take the subject to be God, the thunder of whose wrath is the lion's roar, going forth from his hiding-place to the work of vengeance. Calvin agrees it is God but fixes what he forsakes, his own Temple and city, against a people who had made a proverb of the saying that this was his rest for ever and could not hold together the two truths that he would keep his covenant and still judge his Church. Gill reports the reading that God leaves the temple but allows equally that the conqueror may be meant, leaving Babylon his den and ranging for prey. Clarke stays with the animal, the lion driven from the river banks when they overflow and coming with ravening fierceness into open country.

Ellicott closes on a word. The term for the oppressor's fierceness may by a slight change be read as the sword of oppression; the same word also means dove, and the Latin took it so, the bird having been blazoned, it is said, on the Babylonian standards and become a symbol of their power. Having canvassed it he concludes there is no reason to alter the English. Wesley states the plain effect: the rising up of God out of his covert leaves the land desolate through the fierceness of the enemy, caused by the fierce anger of God.
